extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of Reformation history and church theology
extracted.subtask_description: Close historical and interpretive account of the Erasmus–Luther controversy (free will, authority, moderation) aimed at explaining the theological positions and their social consequences. Focuses on doctrines, argumentative methods, and practical effects in early 16th-century Christianity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth_should_not_always_be_spoken
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus' maxim: 'the truth which seemed likely to make any confusion in the world ought not to be spoken.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erasmus argues that certain theoretical truths (e.g., extreme Augustinian doctrines implying irresistible sin) should be withheld when their public dissemination would disturb public order, promote impiety, or remove incentives for moral effort. He gives examples (claims that would 'open a door to impiety' or make weak men abandon the struggle against the flesh) and explicitly defends withholding truth in some times/places/ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority_and_learning_as_basis_for_interpreting_Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus defends reliance on human authority, learning, and ecclesiastical office to judge Scripture: majorities, ordination, councils, and the recognised life of saints are indicators of the true sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He questions private interpretation by isolated men and stresses probability favoring those ordained or recognised by Church institutions ('chances are much greater that [the Spirit] is to be found among those to whom God has given ordination'). He uses rhetorical questions to rebut claims that private or minority readings trump established authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold_judgment_of_spirits_(internal_and_external)
rubrics_metrics.description: Luther's criterion: spirits/opinions are to be tested by a twofold judgment — an internal judgment (personal, by the Holy Spirit) and an external judgment (public, exercised by the ministry and Church with Scripture as judge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Luther allows private Christians an 'internal clearness' for personal assurance, but insists that for judging doctrines affecting others' salvation there must be an 'external' public judgment by Church ministers and the ministry of the Word, using Scripture to try spirits. This distinguishes private conviction from public doctrinal adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation_between_extremes_as_practical_policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church's practical policy: steer a middle course between Pelagian and Augustinian extremes to preserve moral order and avoid doctrinal positions that undermine social/ethical life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Church historically condemned extreme Pelagian assertions while reverencing Augustine, yet avoided adopting the most extreme Augustinian conclusions; this moderation was pragmatic: it maintained a workable moral system (providing means to avert consequences of evil) and avoided doctrinal positions that would rob men of responsibility or disrupt public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge_doctrines_by_practical_moral_effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines may be assessed by their practical effects: even illogical or extreme theology (e.g., Augustinian predestination) can be justified if it 'works' to recall men to sin-awareness and moral regeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that although Augustinianism 'may have been illogical,' it 'worked' where other means failed by producing some of the most resolute moral agents. Thus efficacy in producing moral purpose is a legitimate evaluative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow_some_role_to_free_will_(Erasmus_non_nihil_position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Erasmus' moderate doctrinal criterion: assign man 'some share' (non nihil) in good actions while recognising the primacy of divine grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He recommends a middle solution allowing grace to provide the initial and final causes, while admitting a secondary role for human will in the progress of action (analogy: grace as principal cause, will as secondary cause). This is offered as a way to avoid both pride and despair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_private_reliance_on_unverified_'Spirit'_claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Skepticism toward claims that the 'witness of the Spirit' alone settles Scripture's meaning for public doctrine; question how one knows they possess the Spirit rather than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erasmus challenges the circularity of 'we have the Spirit because we say we have it' and points to the problem of relying on private assertions of spiritual authority—prompting appeal to learning, life, miracles, or institutional proof rather than uncorroborated private revelation.
